entries.text: A.   The Mennonite Camp

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why don't we start recording now then? We're at Stop 1' on the tour and Gene can you tell me where the Mennonite Camp was located, what you were told?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, as far as I know it was right up this road off to the right when I ... first time I ever saw it there wasn't even no buildings left. All you could see was just indents and stuff where they were and their orchards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the orchards planted by the Mennonites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know they were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you tell me about what year you saw that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, that was in '40's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear any stories about the Mennonites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.2

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How do you know Mennonites were there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My folks told me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any stories or any other things about the Mennonites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's all I know is that they lived there and they couldn't ... there wasn't enough to make a living so they starved out and left.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did your folks tell you about what year that was about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so you went there in the 1920's and looked over there at it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the 1920's was when I was born.   In 1923.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: John Blasch (1883-1964) was the son of German immigrants, orphaned at age 8 or 9. He married Ethel Mabel Boyer (1891-1985) of Suver, Oregon in 1917. Their children were Frederick Arthur (1918-1962); Lawrence Edward (1922-1989); Mary Louise (1924-****) Turner; Anna Gertrude (1929-****); and Alma Maxine (1932-1988). John and Ethel were divorced in 1945 and both remarried in later years. The Blasch home in which the children were born still exists in 1994, and is curently being used as a barn along Robison Road in Benton County.

entries.text: Yeah, it was probably ... three miles from here.

entries.text: Oh, about three miles so it would be right at the base of the [Coffin] Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you go to the other side and then there's a road that cuts to the left. I think there's a cross road up there. He lived right in there, he ... Soap Creek run through their place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. Did he get it from his folks [John], or did he buy the place by himself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, his folks lived there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he lived with his folks and worked for Sheppard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he have any brothers or sisters?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he had another brother [none] and sister [one] or something like that. They were out of our district, too, I just ... I just knew him more or less when we went to high school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you went to high school with /Lawrence] Blasch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he's your age?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay and then ... can you think of anything else about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He didn't have one eye or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, two. [laughs]

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: G.   Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know all he did was he just farmed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dobrinin?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he live in that house right there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the house is gone. It was right here where these trees are.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, where these trees are is where the Dobrinin [Mike] place was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right in here probably where that barn is or shed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where the red shed is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was his house taken away with Camp Adair then too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Dobrinins, they owned the land and far,ned out through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then Camp Adair came in and wiped it off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there an orchard here that they had, a family orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember there being one in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you go to school with the Dobrinins?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this would be the outer edge of the Tampico School District?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many Idds' did they have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. Six, I guess; six or seven [Agnes, Fannie, Mary, Charlie, Annie].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Dobrinin do anything other than farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember him doing anything else.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any particular religion among these families here? Did eveiybody go to the same church?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they go to any church?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they all had their separate churches they went to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you 'd see the kids in school maybe, and some of them; you'd see in church?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was none of these that went to our church.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Which church did you go to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Immanuel Lutheran in Albany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so you went a long way to church?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. About ten miles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't know. Because that's where we started going and we always went there. Either Albany or Corvallis was the closest towns.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So anybody that went to church had to go to Corvallis or Albany?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was ... there were cemeteries through here, or family burial grounds

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's none here that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. None in this neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not right here, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: HOw abow this side of the hill? The west side of the hill. Was this all young fir in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. This was all timber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it looks about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On this farm here where you say people farmed, what kinds of crops did they raise?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mostly wheat and oats, rye grass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Any cattle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, everybody had their cows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about chickens? Were there any chicken ranches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cows and chickens and ... everybody had ... they owned cows and their own chickens.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any problem with animals like opossums, or raccoons, or jack rabbit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any oposswns in this country at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. No opossums.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when they came in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember what year it was, but I remember when they got started why there was ... you see a lot of them pretty quick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I heard they came in with the CCC's; people brought them from the South.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, that could be. I never did see any as long as we lived out here on the ranch here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. How about raccoons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and a lot of skunk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A lot of skunks? How about deer, deer populations?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was deer all over but not near as thick then as they are now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A lot more deer now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any elk?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Black bear?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never seen any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cougar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bobcats?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there were some around. I've seen some up here when I was hunting one day.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the birds? There are quite afew hawks now. Were there a lot of hawics in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was ... well, yeah, but everybody used to shoot them then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The hawks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, hawks and owls.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's probably more hawks, owls, and deer now than there was then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There used to be a lot of pheasants and a lot of quail here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when the pheasants died out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was pretty good yet when we left in the 40's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I hunted here in the '50's when I was a kid and in the '60's, so there was still

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what killed them off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Same thing that it was down in the [Willamette] Valley, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know; they said they got a disease and all died out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any foxes in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There used to be a lot of grey fox.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Grey fox.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Before we left a red fox just started coming in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was told by Bessie Murphy that the foxes killed off the pheasants; the foxes got out of control.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. You think it was more like disease, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Soap Creek, did you fish that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Catch very many fish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, the biggest one I ever got was thirteen and a half inches, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any of the adults fish or just the kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, my dad fished too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: W1zat was the most you ever got in a day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Quite a few.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Over fifty?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, no, not that many, I don't think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Weren't you worried about getting a ticket?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it's been a long time ago. You can't do it anymore, can't even hardly fmd a fish in the creek anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was a lot more fish in the creek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, nobody else ever fished it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What ... was there anything other than rainbow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was cutthroat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any rainbow then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not at first.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How'd they get in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They planted them in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there rainbow when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A few; they got started then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they take over from the cutthroat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you can't hardly get a cutthroat anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it's native cutthroats.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To start with and then they went to rainbow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that thirteen and a half incher a cutthroat or rainbow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it was a cutthroat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Which do you like to catch more?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Any kind.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, did you li/ce seeing the rainbows come in, or did it bother you one way or the other?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It didn't make any difference, they just done better.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, there was more fish once they got the rainbow in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there crawdads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Periwinkles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there used to be a lot of crawdads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ear them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you put out traps for them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not, caught them with a hook and line.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about duth and geese?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Never hunted for them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A few wood ducks come in the creek when ... there was a lot of acorns.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about porcupines?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've never seen one, my uncle saw one up on the hill one time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there has been some porcupines but not real common?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they're not common.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about boomers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grouse?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, mountain beaver [Aplodontia rz(a]?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I've never seen any of them in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about grouse, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there's grouse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there as many now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I couldn't say that, because I don't go up in here very often anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you grouse hunt when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, occasionally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there quite a few?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In certain places there was ... did pretty good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the ... on the migrations on the geese, would there be noticeably a lot more geese in those days than now or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They just flew over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just didn't pay much attention?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they never stayed in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this wasn't a stop for migratory birds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about ... eagles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Never saw any eagles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What are we missing, Jan, mentioned every major fish, bird and ... jack rabbits?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There used to be quite a few jack rabbits.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they a problem?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they didn't really hurt that much. There was quite a lot. You'd get to harvesting a field and you get to the end ... near the inside where you'd be about to finish it, there'd be quite a few rabbit sometimes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Miat would you do with them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just chase them, kill them and eat them or kill them. We'd never eat them, but

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's ... do you recall dWere,u kinds of rabbits, other than the jack rabbit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just the jack rabbit and a few cotton tails.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall anything called a brush bunny, kind of a black short haired rabbit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's probably a little cotton tail, isn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I just had somebody tell me about them. [See Monograph #6, James Hanish.}

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's all I've ever seen. I've just seen a few cotton tails and then the regular jack rabbit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you familiar with djjj'ere,u kinds of moles or mice or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they had regular ... the same kind of mice you've got now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Field mice?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, field mice and regular house mice and kangaroo mice.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A few wood rats.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you have problems with those in the house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know. We always found them down in the sloughs and stuff like that, they would be building wood ... great big wood nests in a tree around an old fence rail fences and stuff like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about nutria?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. They weren't here yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And no beaver?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No beaver when we left. After the Camp [Adair] came in, I went down the creek fishing then and there was beaver in there then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that because people stopped trapping?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think the beaver just moved back up in this country again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about otter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never seen any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so the beaver came in after Camp Adair. The rainbow probably came ... starting to come in the laze '20's, early '30's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The pheasant were here when you were a kid and disappeared maybe in the '60's or '70's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there used to be a lot of bobwhite here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's bobwhite?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bobwhite and then the California quail came in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they still here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know it there's any bobwhite left anyplace anymore hardly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then the red fox. The first one I seen of them was in the, oh, late '30's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they get here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Some of these hound people turned them loose.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For sport?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the grey fox?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they was already ... I think they are native here, because I used to trap them. The red fox I caught I didn't know what it was. When I took it home and got to skinning it, I found a chain around it's neck.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was like apet?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, somebody ... it got away from somebody or what it was. I caught two that year and that's the first ones we ever seen. Didn't even know what they were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about coyote?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a few; there weren't no problem much then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No wolves then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any other animals?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.text: H.   Subsistance and Specialty Farming

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're at a gate, and we've just come down the hill, what's the mileage here, Jan?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you think this might have been Wiles' line, this old fence line coming up this corner here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any buildings, or any old apple orchards, or anything off to the right [west] here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember any ever being there, but I think somebody said there was a house there at one time, but I can't ... I never did see anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To the west of us here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what they told you about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't even remember that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would Wiles be the person that might know?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's possible.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No name associated with it or anything, just an old house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the left here, is the cut off to Coffin Butte, is that an old road there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's the original road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: An original road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any houses or anything particular off to our left here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this somebody's field?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, this right here was Dobrinin's and you get down here is where Lloyd

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Stambaugh [son of Joseph and Emma] used to own some down in   down below there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So if we took the road to the left, we be coming onto Stambaugh 's place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I think there's a house between there or two, but I can't remember. I don't know who owns ... who lived in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did Coffin Butte look like in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It looked just the same that it does now except that it didn't have those roads and the big holes in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How far down was Stambaugh 's house off that turn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just this side of Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so you'd turn here on the left and you'd keep going and right before you cross Soap Creek you'd hit

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Stambaugh's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Stambaugh 's. Was that a farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he used to raise Harding grass there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Harding grass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's that used for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who did he sell itto?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't even know that, that was so many years ago, I didn't ... never ... nobody hardly ever raised that kind of stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. So it was a specialty crop?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were any of these farmers educated at Oregon State [University]?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I couldn't say.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they work with the [OSU] Extension service?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were ... so when they did something like Harding grass, it was maybe an experiment with Oregon State and maybe not?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It could have been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: W!iy do you remember that, what makes you remember that.?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's just ... extra grass, it never was grown any place else around here at the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he had kind of a reputation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of a house did he live in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just an old board house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not a vely fancy one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were most of these houses pretty substantial or were they pretty old and worn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, a lot of them were fairly old already.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would people maintain them pretty good?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they didn't take ... much care of them. A lot of them wasn't even painted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were just board color and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just board.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kind of worn out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Rough boards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And would they have a barn with all the houses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most of them did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And an outhouse or two?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Woodshed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 'What other kinds of buildings would they have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not much, just what they had to have. Just a barn and a house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did everybody have a car?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think at that time they did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were these roads rocked?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So what kinds of cars were the family cars?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, a regular car that people drove in those years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It wasn't like Model T or anything, it would be an Oldsmobile or Pontiac

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was more ... you know, a lot of Model T and stuff in those years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would people ... what kind of tractors would they use?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When I was a kid they didn't even have tractors yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did they use?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, just a regular work horse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No brand name or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Laughs] Well, there probably was on them but

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, when you were a kid people were farming this area with horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A plow and what other kinds offobs did they do?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They got plow, disc, and harrow and they had a drill to sow with.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they mow hay or run balers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wasn't no balers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How was hay stored; how was that stored?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was all ... you would have to cut with a mower and then rake it, and shock it and then you haul it in with a wagon, put it in the barn. It was all loose hay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So everybody had work horses, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And ... how many milk cows would an average family have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't know. Six or seven probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How much would they raise for beef?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just raise some of the ... some of their calves for beef.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would people pay their taxes with; what crops would they raise to get money with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anything that they could make off of anything. Sell a few eggs, sell cream.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Apples?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never knew of anybody selling apples.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about cherries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Any orchard crops?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sheep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there were sheep. Some sheep and a few goats.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, Just kind of nickel and dime, however

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, any way you could make some money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anybody have trouble paying their taxes around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it wasn't very easy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was pretty tough?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was pretty rough then in them years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you ... what are the first years that you remember about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, probably the '30's on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about when your folks first arrived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [I can't] ... remember back that far.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Everybody old enough to remember back that far died.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you're just running out of people.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If we don't get your memories then we've lost all the memory.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know, you're not going to get much from me, either, though.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we've already got quite a lot. You'd be surprised. Can you remember ... could you see any houses off in this direction here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, just up here was those houses I was telling you about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, did that hill in front of us there have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How aboia the hill behind us?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know if there was any name to any of them or not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember Forest Peak [called Steele Hill, Writsmans Hill, or (Francis) Writsmans Butte]?
bracketed_corrections: [called Steele Hill, Writsmans Hill, or (Francis) Writsmans Butte]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, Coffin Butte so far as you know

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Coffin Butte is really the only one that I really knew a name of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And Soap Creek, any other landmarks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, up Soap Creek from the house, you could see that one kind of a bald hill up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did they call it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not sure if they ... is that [Arnold] Writsman's Butt& up in that area someplace?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've heard of a place called Writsman 's Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: I.   The Old Swimming Hole

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is where we used to come swimming right down here a lot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. So the swimming hole's right off on the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: just below the bridge down here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Would all the kkL in the neighborhood go there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Those that lived right in here close.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this knob up on our left, the Hugharz6 homestead, did anybody have a house up there?

He established a Donation Land Claim to the west of Coffin Butte in 1846 with his wife, Martha "Anna" (Henderson) Hughart (1808- 1846), and their children Eliza J. (1828-1849) Smith (she married fellow pioneer, Green Berry Smith in 1848); David E. (1830-1855);

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's where the Wiles house was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Wiles house was on

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right up on the hill by them trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of a house was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was a big house and then he had a great big windmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wind,nill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. With a big tank way up on top up in the tower.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the only windmill in the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the only one I can think of around here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the windmill right on that hill right next to his house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was it used for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Water for the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that something they built; was it a new one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was there as long as I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did he farm this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had mostly a dairy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dairy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was his dairy barn at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just over on the ... down below the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How far off the hill there maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, maybe from the house probably 300 feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Three hundred feet on the down hill side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many head did he have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he have a creamery?

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Martha Ann (1833-1895) Wiles (married to fellow pioneer, John Wiles); William T. (1836-1857); and Mary F. (1839-1856). Anna Hughart is reputed to have been the first white woman buried in Benton County.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he sold the whole milk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he didn't make cheese or anything else?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dkl he have any other crops; raise hay for the cows?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember anymore whether he did that or not. He never farmed very much because he had a big enough dairy that kept him busy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was afull time dairy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he run cows on both sides of the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember that anymore either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he own pretty much up to the [Coffin] Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he had a pretty large farm in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was pretty good size. I think his line fence was pretty close to where that road cuts across down here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cuts across the west side of the Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: John Wiles, is that the son?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did ... were those kids your friends?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would you do for fun?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, go hunt and fish.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you hunt for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pheasants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we never hunted pheasants that much. We was small enough all we had were B.B. guns. We'd just go out, shoot birds and stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Azything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Shoot at cans. You know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Go fishing in the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you swain down here, how far below the bridge was the swimming hole?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, 100 feet, just a little ways down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have aname?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just the swimming hole?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would you fish at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The whole creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Below the swimming hole and up above it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From here clear up to Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Sulphur Springs, would your family ever go up there as a group?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Once in a while we went up there, picnic.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would other families in the neighborhood go there

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never did go when there was a big family deal, I mean, a neighborhood picnic.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you hear about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know if I've ever even heard of there being a neighborhood picnic up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would people go on the Fourth of July?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We always stayed home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have fireworks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Other neighbors?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no our relations all came out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you went picnicking at Sulphur Springs, what kind of things would you take?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a regular picnic lunch.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cold chicken?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably. That and sandwiches.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Watennelons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Beer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I wasn't old enough then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would your parents take you up, or just the kids go up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we had to go up with the parents then. I wasn't hardly old enough to drive when I was

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You didn't take horses up or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it would be ... in those days the kids didn't have horses or travel much by horseback?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not much, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So f your parents didn't drive you, you'd walk up and down the creek or walk to the swimming hole or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Other than swimming, and fishing and hunting, would there be gaines, play softball or catch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just at school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there'd be organized games at school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about ... were there swings or ropes, did they have.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we had a play shed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was that located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right there where the road is by the school house. See that road; they dozed it out when they built the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was the play shed for like the neighborhood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For the school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, did you build tree houses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I never did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would all the kids pretty much do the same things, do them together in groups or stick to your own family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Usually stayed pretty well alone. Too far to go to all the neighbors. This was about the closest neighbor I had right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wiles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this your best friend ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Good as any of them I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you stayed home would you do much reading?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Listen to the radio?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, some. There wasn't much on radios then either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about painting or

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Work with clay?

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q

entries.text: J.   A Fatal Accident at Govier's Mill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the name of the family that lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Studach's [Jacob].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What mileage are we on here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Eleven point nine. What kind offamily was that? How many kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see. They had three, two boys [John and Alfred] and a girl.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pretty girl?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, sure [laughs].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said there was a bridge went to their house. Where did the bridge go?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The same place the house did, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I mean, where was it located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right where there's a deer trail there or cow trail.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was their ... and the bridge, what would it cross -- this ditch here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so this was ditched out about the same at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was a deep ditch through here as long as I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have any problem with flooding from the creek here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They raised bees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. The only bees I ever saw around here was when some guy from Albany brought some and put them down on our place. That Hines,. Ralph Hines, was a honey man then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would he bring them up eveiy year to pollinate your crop or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he'd just bring them down to have a place to put them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would he give you any honey for the deal?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he gave us honey once in a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Studach's, what was their house, how far to our ... to the west was it located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, just right there where those trees are. Just this side of them. See, what seventy-five feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a large house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. No, it was just a small house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that on the map there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just a plain board house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they called it the Studach 's house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They were the first ones that I knew of that lived there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they build it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I couldn't say that. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they live here the whole time you were here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he got killed and then ... a [Albert] Zundt lived there for awhile. And then there was some others ... I can't remember the names of those that lived in there after that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did Studach get killed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Saw mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Which sawmill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Govier's [Alvie].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Govier 's saw mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Had a log roll over him, I guess.

entries.text: What happened to his family after that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They moved to Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wife remariy or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know she never did. I went to [Corvallis] High School with the kids there then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have insurance in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they had kind of a tough time after their dad died?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] What kind of a name is Studach?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Swiss.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, were there very many Swiss families here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Studach 's were the only ones?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he an immigrant, did he have a Swiss accent?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, gosh, I don't know. I was just a little ... wasn't very big there when he got killed so I ... I never, didn't really know him that well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody get blamed for that or anything, was that big news around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a bad accident?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just something that happened.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have an orchard through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just the trees that are here now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many acres?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, let's see, it ran from there over ... well, right up there's the other line of the fence, and another one was on Wiles', and then it went up here and joined our place. What is there? Forty acres in there or something like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it went from Wiles and then forty acres, or Studach 's, and then after they moved out then Zundt moved in and was that a family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he was a bachelor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bachelor? Did he work in a mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he worked there for Govier's, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long after Studdock got killed, how long did the family stay here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think they were here very long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just left almost immediately?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they didn't have nothing ... they couldn't live out here so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: After Zundt left, then a few other people moved in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then was this building still here when Camp Adair

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was destroyed along with the other buildings when they put in Camp Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Everything that was on the main camp was torn down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about did they have a barn here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he just had a little shop.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a little shop. What kind of a shop wa it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't even know what he had it for, whether it was just a place to park a car or what it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any buildings off here on these

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never did see anything over in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would this still be Wiles' property over here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That goes up to where these trees start.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a single

entries.text: And she was older than you, so

entries.text: Now the Beals ... this property here on our left was this the Beals?   What kind ofproperty was this?

entries.text: What did they call it, Beal 's swamp?

entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did he do with the rest of it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was all timber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he log it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think some of it was logged. Now he never logged; he cut everything for cord wood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And did he live here all the way up 'til Camp Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ithinkso.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he have any kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he had two girls.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pretty girls? [Laughs]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not as good as the St

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If you say so. I never seen them very much; they were just little girls.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Way younger than you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I was kInd of wondering which one of the family

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, see from here they went to Soap Creek School.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So these didn't go to the same school as you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, okay. I was kind of wondering why you didn't know these girls as well as you did the ones on the other side there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The other ones went to your school and then these kids here went the other way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and they were younger than you. Do you know where the Mallows moved after the War or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Moved out of Albany, I think someplace, or Corvallis ... I don't know ... He died, I think both of them. They have a daughter [Marie] that lives there someplace around Albany though.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know her name now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right now I can't think of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, maybe that's something maybe you can look up or something, so jf we want to find ow' a little bit more abow the Mallows and there'd be somebody to contact.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything particular happening around this house or coming over here for any event?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have orchards or go hunting with them or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I came over to go fishing with their boy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they had a son too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Two boys and a girl ... I mean the early people [Griffm].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, the ones you can't remember their na,nes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I don't know why I can't think of it, I knew them real well, but it's just you've got me scared out. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we can look it up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] It will come to mind, I'm sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, those are the types of things we can look up, but ... so people that lived before you can remember them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you used to go fishing with the boy.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I knew Mallow too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. And then did you ever come over and spend the night or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But just go fishing or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he was about your age?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: M.   Beef Barn Road

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're on the beef barn road and there wasn't nothing here. This was Mallow's place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would be

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had a bridge, but right now I can't remember just right where it was anymore now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we can probably find that on an old photograph, but there was a track and bridge and then he'd get up in the hills right through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the family before   what did you say ... Max and Guy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't think of their names. [Griffin]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] John and Lola and Guy and Max. And what was his [Guy] wife's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hazel.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] Hazel.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now did they farm this area, the earlier ... before Mallow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he done some ... he farmed in through here. See, this went clear up here to this other fence up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so they ... but would that bridge have been put in by Mallows or would they have already had one in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That I can't ... I think there was ... there was a bridge there ... through there already.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. Was there any swimming holes or any special places along the creek through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wherever you wanted to swim.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but the one swimming hole you showed me down there ... was the main one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's where it was handy for all the kids around there to go. See, when I was down here fishing, I just ... any place I come to deep enough to swim then I'd go swimming.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any deep holes in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, nothing real deep, nothing over my head.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, three orfourfoot was about as deep as it got?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it muddy, or cold, or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cold!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it wasn't muddy; it was a nice clear creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you never found any Indian artifacts and other than those elephant teeth was there any fossils or anything unusual through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I never did see any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No beaver, just a regular creek ... did it look pretty much in those days like it looks now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still looks pretty similar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it hasn't changed much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: N.   Stage Stop Lane

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're at Stage Stop Lane.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The guy that built that up in there

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] Thirteen

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: used to be a sheriff at Albany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A sheriff of Albany moved here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what year he did that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. It was when we still lived here, when he built that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, this place is an old place; this goes back to the thirties?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, something like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And a sherzfffrom Albany built it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he worked for the Sheriff Department

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Does that family still own it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't the slightest idea. I haven't heard   had any contact with anybody from there for years ... for a long, long time now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they moved ... they were here the same time the Mallows were here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so. And it's just about that time there when... I can't remember really when they built in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's the mileage here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] Thirteen point seven.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Thirteen point seven. This driveway was just put in at that time when he built?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Asfaraslknow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any orchards or anything through here that you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now that road there comes down from the Dunn Forest with a gate, do you know was that in here in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's new?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's new.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. A mail box is up there on the left, is there a reason ... does that belong to this place here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that might be where the road went that went up to the house. I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this might be a new road right here, Stage Stop Lane?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall the name of that man?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Kirk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kirk?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And Kirk moved in here in the 1930's, took some. undeveloped property and built a house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I guess he built, I don't know if there was a house ... I can't remember there being a house, but if there was one ... there could have been, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You don't remember anybody here before him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there a reason to stop by that mail box up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you know anything about the Kirk family; did they have kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Idon'tthinkso.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, maybe was he retired or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he keep working in Albany?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he was at Albany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he raise any crops or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All these fields here

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This here was all Mallow's, their last.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I can't think of anything else here. Can you think of anything else?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: O.   The Old Schoolhouse

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You can park right out here. This is where that old school used to be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, this is the Kirk driveway here probably. And was that Kirk's house right there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that's where it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So that house would go back at least to the 1 930's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ithinkso.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] I think so, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It looks like an older house f not real old. Now those oak must have been here in those days.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that fir tree. Can you remember anything else about this here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there more oaks on the hill or look about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think there was more brush and stuff around here at that time, but I don't know, I can't ... it's hard to tell anymore, it's ... stuff changed so much up through here. You know, different places, I don't remember what it was like anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were these fences along this side here, were they split rail in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was wire fence then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it barbed wire or woven wire like this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, woven.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they look pretty similar now to what it used to be?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about along the slough through there and that area, was that

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was all wire fence.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was all fenced off too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And was woven wire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just kind of like the stuff we're looking at right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Were the trees about the same through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I don't think anybody's bothered any of the trees along the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've got kind of a drainage, a little marsh area off here to our right, do you know anything about that at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it's just a ditch coming down off the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jan, what's the mileage right here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] Thirteen point nine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, 13.9, we're looking at three fir trees and then behind them north and east about 150 ftet is an oak tree and in between is a swale with some brush, can you tell me where the school used to be in relation to those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think the school used to set right out in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right between us and the oak tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ithinkso.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] Where that little lump is out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, apparently.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up on the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right close to that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever go to that [Soap Creek] school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it still standing when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Because after they built the other school they moved out some people that lived in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember that family's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not any more.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they farm around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I think he worked out for a living.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could he have worked at like Govier's, or something, or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what he done. I think some of the time this guy worked for Mallow, cut wood, and drove truck, and stuff like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Worked for Mallow? Did he have any land to speak of?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He didn't. All he had was just that house; I think he rented the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. How did you know it was a school before then? Did you go there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. When they left down there they went to school here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, this is the kids when you said they went up Soap Creek to go to this one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they went to this one, and see, they built that new one up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was the one before the new one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so maybe the picture I've got in the book that shows a school built in 1899 might have been right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Could have been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so this ... was this called the Soap Creek School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I suppose.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You can't remember a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't remember any names on that stuff in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is why the Mallow kids, why you didn't know them so well ... they came to this school here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did this look like a regular school house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was more like a ... just like a house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have a little deal for the bell or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember. I don't think it did. It might have, but I don't remember any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you ... how far between us and the oak was it, maybe halfway or most of the way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, probably three-fourths of the way down to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And was that building there up until Camp Ad.air?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Asfaraslknowitwas. Ithinkitwas yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably pretty. .. . I bet you it's in there where that mound is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. How about those three trees there, do you know anything about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No story, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's a dump through here somewhere, are we coming up on that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. There isn't any dump that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You showed me some spot down here below the road where you said there was a dump at some time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, okay. We 'lljust

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: P.   Elmer Govier's House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. The house that we couldn't remember their name was the Griffin house. And then the little swale just past the school house site, the family that moved in there dumped their stuff and the school stuff over the hill there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know if the school dumped it in there, but I know they did. I saw stuff in there when those people lived there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they dump it right next to the road or just off to the side of their house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In a swale beside the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, we're ... this house here, do you remember how Griffins spelled their name? Griffus or Grzffen [Griffin]?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: G-r-i-f-f-e-n, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: E-n. Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Jan] And that was Hazel and Guy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're in front of... what house is this called? Who's house was this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Elmer Govier.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he the one that owned the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. He was a brother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The brother. Do you know how long this family was here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were here as long as I can remember, up to the time the Camp took over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, are there any relatives of Elmer's still alive?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had some daughters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And do you know where they might live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's still   do you remember any of their married names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'll probably ... maybe think of one pretty quick. I know one, but I can't think of it right now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got a list of some Goviers and their married names, so I think we could probably find one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You probably can get it from ... there's a bunch of Goviers live up here yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Elmer Govier farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so this area out through here then was probably the Govierfann?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it went Govier, Mallow, Glender brothers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wiles and Beals? That would be kind of the main farmers through this area in the '30's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, where was the old barn at here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It used to be over in there, I think. Someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where that old building is right there now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Back there someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, the road cuts out here and goes out on a right angle and the old road Ic. 1853] used to go from about that corner and run straight. Here's a place where they took a straight road and put in a corner. Do you know anything about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is just the way it was when you were a kid, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I can remember it's always been like this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Anything Jan?

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Q.   The Hildebrand Fire

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the name of this family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hildebrand [Bill].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they farm here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see, yeah, I think they more or less farmed. Before them a [Lee] Brown lived here. They were older people. The originals.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know why they moved?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.   Couldn't make a living here, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know about when they moved?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, gosh, I couldn't say.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember them, the Browns [Lee and Gertrude]?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: lust barely.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So maybe they moved about 1930?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've seen them. I think it was Lyle [Norris Lyle Brown] was the boy and there was old ... the original place ... house is back up over here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so this place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then they built down here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there anything left of the Brown place when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a nice old home?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was pretty nice house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did they abandon it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This one here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The one over on the hill?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't know, that ... there wasn't much left of that anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just rotting down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was too far off the road I think to get back and forth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would they get there, would they get there through this gate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know where the road was. There's a road up here that goes back up in there now and that goes right up to it now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tothe old home?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But was that taken out when Camp Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There used to be parts of the old barn and stuff up there yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this one right here, can you tell me the stoiy on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just that Hildebrand bought it from Brown and then when it burned up, it burned three people up in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the year of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see, it should have been   I think I was going to high school then, '38, something like that, '38 or '39.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who died in that fire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The woman and one of the boys and one of their uncles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One of the uncles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did ... who survived it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: One boy and the Mister.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they [Hildebrands] hurt or anything in the fire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were burnt.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pretty bad?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the boy was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is he still around?

entries.speaker: A
